claims.evidence: Supported by visual evidence in Figures 3C and 3D showing correlation of preferred phases between conditions.

claims.claim: 139 out of 842 neurons (16.5%) showed positive modulation of firing rates by visual inputs.
claims.source: Positive modulation by visual inputs was observed ~4 times more frequently than negative modulation (139 out of 842 or 16.5% positively modulated neurons; 32 out of 842 or 3.8% negatively modulated neurons at significance level alpha = 0.05; data from 15 mice).
claims.evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis of neuronal responses across 842 neurons from 15 mice.

claims.claim: 32 out of 842 neurons (3.8%) showed negative modulation of firing rates by visual inputs.
claims.source: Positive modulation by visual inputs was observed ~4 times more frequently than negative modulation (139 out of 842 or 16.5% positively modulated neurons; 32 out of 842 or 3.8% negatively modulated neurons at significance level alpha = 0.05; data from 15 mice).
claims.evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis of neuronal responses across 842 neurons from 15 mice.

claims.claim: The running speed-dependent gains in firing rate of MEC speed cells remain unaltered during the absence of visual inputs.
claims.source: In summary, these data demonstrate that the running speed-dependent gains in firing rate of MEC speed cells remain unaltered during the absence of visual inputs, even if mean firing rates and the slopes of speed tuning curves change substantially.
claims.evidence: Supported by analysis of speed response curves after normalization within conditions (Figure 5D and Table 6).

claims.claim: No significant difference was observed between speed responses of positively speed-modulated neurons in the dark condition compared to the light condition after correcting for changes in mean firing rate.
claims.source: In particular, no significant difference was observed between speed responses of positively speed-modulated neurons in the dark condition compared to the light condition (Table 6).
claims.evidence: Supported by statistical analysis presented in Table 6.

claims.claim: Speed scores of all speed-modulated neurons were not significantly changed between light and dark conditions on the population level.
claims.source: Likewise, speed scores (Pearson's correlation coefficient between firing rate and running speed) of all speed-modulated neurons were not significantly changed between light and dark conditions on the population level (p=0.912, n = 164, Kolmogorov-Smirnov test) (Figure 5E) and were highly correlated between light and dark conditions on the single cell level (R = 0.86) (Figure 5F).
claims.evidence: Supported by statistical testing (Kolmogorov-Smirnov test) and correlation analysis, with visual representation in Figures 5E and 5F.

claims.claim: Spatial periodicity of grid cell firing was low in the initial dark session and strongly increased during the first light session.
claims.source: We found that spatial periodicity of grid cell firing was low—but not completely eliminated—in the initial dark session and then strongly increased during the first light session (Figure 6A & B).
claims.evidence: Supported by visual evidence in Figures 6A and 6B showing firing rate maps and grid scores across sequential sessions.

claims.claim: After initial orientation in light, spatial periodicity of grid cell firing decreased again after removal of visual inputs but remained significantly higher than in the initial dark session.
claims.source: Interestingly, after this initial orientation, spatial periodicity of grid cell firing decreased again after removal of visual inputs, but remained significantly higher than in the initial dark session (Chi-square = 10.89, p=0.0043, n = 9 cells from two mice, Friedman test; post-hoc tests revealed p<0.05 comparing initial dark and light, and initial dark and second dark sessions).
claims.evidence: Supported by statistical analysis (Friedman test with post-hoc comparisons) of grid scores across sequential dark-light-dark sessions.

claims.claim: Grid cell field centers remained stable, but grid fields appeared wider during complete darkness.
claims.source: We found that grid cell field centers remained stable, but grid fields appeared wider during complete darkness (Figure 6C).
claims.evidence: Supported by visual comparison of firing rate maps in Figure 6C.

claims.claim: Grid scores and spatial information of grid cells showed significant decreases during darkness.
claims.source: Quantification of spatial periodicity and spatial precision of grid cell firing by computing grid scores and spatial information (see Materials and methods) revealed a significant decrease in both spatial periodicity and spatial precision of spike locations (Figure 6D & E).
claims.evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis with visual representation in Figures 6D and 6E.

claims.claim: Spatiotemporal correlation between observed firing rate and expected firing rate from position showed significant reduction during complete darkness.
claims.source: The results show a significant reduction in spatiotemporal correlation during complete darkness (Figure 6F).
claims.evidence: Supported by analysis of spatiotemporal correlation with visual representation in Figure 6F.

claims.claim: Grid scores computed from spike-triggered firing rate maps showed significant decrease in darkness.
claims.source: Nevertheless, we observed a significant decrease in the grid scores computed from spike-triggered firing rate maps (p=0.0354, n = 15 cells, Wilcoxon signed-rank test) (Figure 6—figure supplements 1 and 2A) suggesting that the phase of each grid map remained stable in darkness.
claims.evidence: Supported by statistical analysis (Wilcoxon signed-rank test) of grid scores from spike-triggered firing rate maps.

claims.claim: Grid spacing remained unchanged in darkness (median grid spacing = 42 cm in light and dark).
claims.source: Lastly, we measured the grid spacing in each of the spike-triggered firing rate maps. Grid spacing remained unchanged in darkness (median grid spacing = 42 cm in light and dark, p=1, Wilcoxon signed-rank test, Bayes factor = 0.2005) (Figure 6—figure supplement 2B).
claims.evidence: Supported by quantitative measurements with statistical testing (Wilcoxon signed-rank test) and Bayesian analysis.

claims.claim: Head direction cells maintained their head direction preference in the dark condition.
claims.source: Interestingly, head direction cells maintained their head direction preference in the dark condition (Figure 7A & B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1) suggesting that animals remained oriented within the environment during complete darkness.
claims.evidence: Supported by visual evidence in Figures 7A, 7B and supplementary figure 1 showing maintained preferred head directions.

claims.claim: The mean resultant lengths of head directional firing rate maps were decreased in the dark condition.
claims.source: However, the mean resultant lengths of head directional firing rate maps were decreased in the dark condition (Cohen's d = 0.238, p=0.0337, Wilcoxon signed-rank test) suggesting that the accuracy of head directional tuning was reduced in darkness (Figure 7C).
claims.evidence: Supported by statistical analysis (Wilcoxon signed-rank test with effect size) and visual representation in Figure 7C.

claims.claim: Border scores were significantly decreased during darkness.
claims.source: Border scores were significantly decreased during darkness (Cohen's d = –0.4975, p=0.0325, Wilcoxon signed-rank test) (Figure 7E) suggesting that representations of boundaries in the open-field environment were less accurate during darkness.
claims.evidence: Supported by statistical analysis (Wilcoxon signed-rank test with effect size) and visual representation in Figure 7E.

claims.claim: Grid cell stability measured as spatiotemporal correlation was strongly correlated with the slope of the LFP theta frequency vs. running speed relationship (R = 0.966, p=1.83×10–21).
claims.source: Intriguingly, grid cell stability measured as spatiotemporal correlation of grid cell firing was strongly correlated with the slope of the LFP theta frequency vs. running speed relationship (R = 0.966, p=1.83×10–21, n = 36 (18 time points x two conditions); Figure 8F and Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: Supported by correlation analysis with visual representation in Figure 8F and supplementary figure 1.

claims.claim: The time courses of changes in grid cell stability and the slope of the LFP theta frequency vs. running speed relationship were correlated within light and dark conditions.
claims.source: The time courses of changes in grid cell stability and the slope of the LFP theta frequency vs. running speed relationship were also correlated within light and dark conditions (Light: R = 0.825, p=2.55×10–5, n = 18 time points; Dark: R = 0.490, p=0.039, n = 18 time points) further confirming the link between grid cell stability and the LFP theta frequency to running speed relationship.
claims.evidence: Supported by correlation analysis within each condition separately.

claims.claim: Changes in the y-intercept of the LFP theta frequency vs. running speed relationship were negatively correlated with changes in grid cell stability in the light condition but uncorrelated in the dark condition.
claims.source: In contrast, changes in the y-intercept of the LFP theta frequency vs. running speed relationship as a function of time were negatively correlated with changes in grid cell stability in the light condition (R = –0.633, p=0.0048, n = 18 time points) and uncorrelated to changes in grid cell stability in the dark condition (R = 0.056, p=0.83, n = 18 time points) (Figure 8—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: Supported by correlation analysis with visual representation in supplementary figure 2.

claims.claim: Grid cell firing is a function of velocity signals integrated over past time.
claims.source: Finally, changes in spatial accuracy of grid cell firing on a 10 s time scale suggest that grid cell firing is a function of velocity signals integrated over past time.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the observed slow saturating exponential changes in grid cell spatial accuracy over tens of seconds.

claims.claim: Sensory inputs other than visual inputs can support grid cell firing, though less accurately, in complete darkness.
claims.source: Moreover, we provide evidence that sensory inputs other than visual inputs can support grid cell firing, though less accurately, in complete darkness.
claims.evidence: Supported by observations that grid cells maintain some spatial periodicity in darkness, though with reduced accuracy.

claims.claim: Visual inputs do not alter the running speed-dependent gain in neuronal firing rates.
claims.source: In contrast, visual inputs do not alter the running speed-dependent gain in neuronal firing rates.
claims.evidence: Supported by analysis showing no significant changes in speed response curves after normalization within conditions (Figure 5D, Table 6).

claims.claim: Changes in spatial stability of grid cell firing correlate with changes in a proposed speed signal by local field potential theta frequency.
claims.source: By examining the temporal correlations between grid cell spatial stability and the two proposed speed signals—by firing rate or theta oscillations—we test if observed changes in grid cell firing can be explained by changes in the speed signal by firing rate or changes in the speed signal by LFP theta frequency.
claims.evidence: Supported by correlation analysis showing strong relationship between grid cell stability and LFP theta frequency slope (Figure 8F).

claims.claim: The spatially periodic firing of grid cells in the medial entorhinal cortex is widely recognized as a neuronal correlate of memory-guided and/or self-motion-based spatial navigation.
claims.source: The spatially periodic firing of grid cells in the medial entorhinal cortex (MEC) (Fyhn et al., 2008; Fyhn et al., 2004; Hafting et al., 2005) is widely recognized as a neuronal correlate of memory-guided and/or self-motion-based spatial navigation (McNaughton et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to established literature on grid cells.

claims.claim: Computational models of grid cells suggest that grid cells integrate running direction and traveled distance to maintain a spatially periodic firing pattern during path integration.
claims.source: Based on that idea, computational models of grid cells including attractor network models (Burak and Fiete, 2009; Fuhs and Touretzky, 2006), oscillatory interference models (Blair et al., 2008; Burgess, 2008; Burgess et al., 2007; Hasselmo, 2008; Zilli and Hasselmo, 2010), hybrid models of attractor networks and oscillatory interference (Bush and Burgess, 2014), and probabilistic learning models (Cheung, 2016) suggest that grid cells integrate running direction and traveled distance to maintain a spatially periodic firing pattern during path integration (Gil et al., 2018; Jacob et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to multiple computational modeling studies.

claims.claim: Path integration depends on a velocity signal which depends on vestibular and proprioceptive signals and also moving sensory features such as optic flow.
claims.source: Path integration depends on a velocity signal which depends on vestibular and proprioceptive signals (Chen et al., 2019; Tennant et al., 2018) and also moving sensory features such as optic flow (Campbell et al., 2018; Raudies et al., 2012; Raudies and Hasselmo, 2015).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to studies on velocity signals in path integration.

claims.claim: Any path integration mechanism ultimately suffers from the accumulation of error over distance traveled or elapsed time necessitating error correction by static environmental sensory inputs.
claims.source: However, any path integration mechanism ultimately suffers from the accumulation of error over distance traveled or elapsed time (Kraus et al., 2015; Sreenivasan and Fiete, 2011) necessitating error correction by static environmental sensory inputs (Evans et al., 2016; Giocomo, 2016) such as visual landmark cues (Campbell et al., 2018; Hafting et al., 2005) or environmental boundaries (Barry et al., 2007; Hardcastle et al., 2015) to maintain an accurate representation of relative self-location within a spatial environment.
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to studies on error accumulation in path integration and error correction mechanisms.

claims.claim: Self-motion-based signals such as head direction are necessary for grid cell firing.
claims.source: Self-motion-based signals such as head direction are necessary for grid cell firing (Campbell et al., 2018; Winter et al., 2015b), and grid cell firing persists during darkness with reduced spatial selectivity (Allen et al., 2014; Hafting et al., 2005) reflecting the loss of error correction by visual cues.
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to experimental studies on grid cell firing requirements.

claims.claim: Two recent studies on mice reported a rapid and nearly complete loss of spatially periodic grid cell firing during complete darkness.
claims.source: In contrast, two more recent studies on mice reported a rapid and nearly complete loss of spatially periodic grid cell firing during complete darkness (Chen et al., 2016; Pérez-Escobar et al., 2016) suggesting that spatially periodic grid cell firing and path integration depend on error correction by visual cues.
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to recent studies on mice showing loss of grid cell firing in darkness.

claims.claim: Motion-related interoceptive representations can combine with visual representations to form a single multimodal representation supporting path integration.
claims.source: However, motion-related interoceptive representations, such as proprioceptive, vestibular, and motor efference copy signals, can combine with visual representations to form a single multimodal representation supporting path integration (Tcheang et al., 2011) suggesting that external sensory cues other than visual cues may be sufficient to stabilize grid cells and support path integration.
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to study on multimodal sensory integration in path integration.

claims.claim: Environmental novelty selectively reduces the slope of the LFP theta vs. running speed relationship and results in an increase in grid scale.
claims.source: Interestingly, environmental novelty selectively reduces the slope of the LFP theta vs. running speed relationship (Jeewajee et al., 2008b; Wells et al., 2013) and also results in an increase in grid scale (Barry et al., 2012) as predicted by oscillatory interference models of grid cell firing (Burgess, 2008).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to studies on effects of environmental novelty on theta dynamics and grid scale.

claims.claim: The y-intercept of the LFP theta vs. running speed relationship has been linked to emotion-sensitivity, in particular anxiolysis.
claims.source: In contrast, the y-intercept of the LFP theta vs. running speed relationship has been linked to emotion-sensitivity, in particular anxiolysis (Korotkova et al., 2018; Monaghan et al., 2017; Wells et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to studies linking theta frequency y-intercept to emotional states.

claims.claim: Pharmacological inactivation of MSDB neurons strongly reduces both theta oscillations and spatial periodicity of grid cell firing in the MEC.
claims.source: In contrast to the speed signal by firing rate (Dannenberg et al., 2019; Hinman et al., 2016), the theta oscillatory speed signal depends on the MSDB (Chrobak et al., 1989; Dannenberg et al., 2015; Givens and Olton, 1994; Hinman et al., 2016; Lawson and Bland, 1993), and pharmacological inactivation of MSDB neurons strongly reduces both theta oscillations and spatial periodicity of grid cell firing in the MEC (Brandon et al., 2011; Koenig et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to studies on effects of MSDB inactivation on theta and grid cells.

claims.claim: Passive transportation of rats reduces theta oscillatory power and abolishes both spatially periodic grid cell firing and the speed signal by LFP theta frequency.
claims.source: Furthermore, passive transportation of rats reduces theta oscillatory power and abolishes both spatially periodic grid cell firing and the speed signal by LFP theta frequency (Winter et al., 2015b).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to study on effects of passive transportation on grid cells and theta.

claims.claim: Pharmacological inactivation of the vestibular system or preventing linear/translational head movements abolish the modulation of LFP theta frequency by running speed and are associated with a decrease in the spatial information score and an increase in grid scale.
claims.source: Likewise, pharmacological inactivation of the vestibular system or preventing linear/translational head movements in a virtual reality setup abolish the modulation of LFP theta frequency by running speed and are associated with a decrease in the spatial information score and an increase in grid scale (Chen et al., 2018; Jacob et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to studies on vestibular system and head movement effects on theta and grid cells.

claims.claim: The increase in grid scale observed during path integration on a circular track is associated with a change in the frequency of LFP theta oscillations, but not with a change in the firing patterns of speed and head direction cells.
claims.source: Interestingly, the increase in grid scale observed during path integration on a circular track is associated with a change in the frequency of LFP theta oscillations, but not with a change in the firing patterns of speed and head direction cells (Jacob et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to study on grid scale changes during circular track navigation.

claims.claim: Artificial low-theta stimulation can affect an animal's estimation of linear distance during approaches to a goal zone.
claims.source: Moreover, a recent study demonstrated that artificial low-theta stimulation can affect an animal's estimation of linear distance during approaches to a goal zone (Mouchati et al., 2020) further strengthening a potential link between LFP theta frequency and path integration.
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to study on effects of theta stimulation on distance estimation.

claims.claim: Speed modulation of hippocampal theta frequency has been shown to correlate with spatial memory performance.
claims.source: In addition, speed modulation of hippocampal theta frequency has been shown to correlate with spatial memory performance (Richard et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to study on theta frequency and spatial memory.

claims.claim: Theta signals within the hippocampal formation have been suggested to reflect alterations in sensorimotor integration and the flow of sensory input, as well as distinct cognitive operations.
claims.source: Theta signals within the hippocampal formation have been suggested to not only reflect alterations in sensorimotor integration and the flow of sensory input, but also distinct cognitive operations (Hinman et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to study on theta signals and cognitive operations.

claims.claim: Much of theta physiology and function seems to be shared across rodents and primates including the correlation of theta frequency with movement speed.
claims.source: Furthermore, much of theta physiology and function seems to be shared across rodents and primates including the correlation of theta frequency with movement speed (Goyal et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to study on theta physiology across species.

claims.claim: Increased phase locking has been associated with dynamical switching between encoding and retrieval dynamics.
claims.source: Increased phase locking has been associated with dynamical switching between encoding and retrieval dynamics (Hasselmo et al., 2002; Siegle and Wilson, 2014), memory performance (Liebe et al., 2012; Rutishauser et al., 2010; Schomburg et al., 2014), and spatial cognitive demand (Barry et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to studies on phase locking and cognitive functions.

claims.claim: The number of theta rhythmic neurons increased sharply from 181 during immobility to 287 at the onset of running in the light condition.
claims.source: In the light condition, the number of significantly theta rhythmic neurons increased sharply from 181 during immobility to 287 at the onset of running.
claims.evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis of theta rhythmic neurons as a function of running speed (Figure 2E).

claims.claim: In the dark condition, the number of significantly theta rhythmic neurons sharply increased at the onset of running and then saturated close to the maximal number.
claims.source: In contrast, the number of significantly theta rhythmic neurons sharply increased at the onset of running and then saturated close to the maximal number during darkness (157 during immobility, 322, 326, and 328 out of 339 neurons at higher running speeds) (Figure 2E).
claims.evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 2E.

claims.claim: The ensemble of theta rhythmic neurons decreased with running speed in the light condition but increased to ceiling during the dark condition.
claims.source: These data demonstrate that the ensemble of theta rhythmic neurons decreased with running speed in the light condition but increased to ceiling during the dark condition (Figure 2E) contributing to the stronger synchrony of theta rhythmic firing observed on the population level (Figure 2D).
claims.evidence: Supported by analysis shown in Figures 2D and 2E.

claims.claim: Both the frequency and magnitude of theta rhythmic firing was higher in putative principal neurons compared to putative interneurons.
claims.source: In general, both the frequency and magnitude of theta rhythmic firing was higher in PNs compared to INs (Figure 2—figure supplements 2C and 3C).
claims.evidence: Supported by comparison of theta rhythmic firing properties between cell types shown in supplementary figures.

claims.claim: Changes in theta rhythmic spiking activity as a function of running speed during and between light and dark conditions were similar across grid cells, head direction cells, and border cells.
claims.source: We found that changes in theta rhythmic spiking activity as a function of running speed during and between light and dark conditions were similar across grid cells, head direction cells, and border cells (Figure 2—figure supplements 4, 5 and 6) and indistinguishable from all PNs, indicating that changes in theta rhythmic activity is ubiquitous across different functional cell types in the medial entorhinal cortex.
claims.evidence: Supported by analysis across different functional cell types shown in supplementary figures.

claims.claim: Changes in firing rates and theta rhythmic firing are primarily driven by changes in net excitatory input from visual cortex and do not reflect changes in the perception of the spatial aspects of the environment.
claims.source: Taken together, these data suggest that changes in firing rates and theta rhythmic firing are primarily driven by changes in net excitatory input from visual cortex and do not reflect changes in the perception of the spatial aspects of the environment.
claims.evidence: Inferred from observations that spatially non-informative light stimulation produces similar effects as light-dark transitions (Figure 4E & F).

claims.claim: Changes in retinal stimulation due to changes in the amount of spatially non-informative light hitting the retina are sufficient to explain the observed changes in mean firing rates of MEC neurons.
claims.source: In summary, these data demonstrate that the changes in retinal stimulation due to changes in the amount of spatially non-informative light hitting the retina after transitioning from dark to light and vice versa are sufficient to explain the observed changes in mean firing rates of MEC neurons.
claims.evidence: Supported by optogenetic control experiments showing similar effects with spatially non-informative light (Figure 4E & F).

claims.claim: Animals need an initial orientation in the environment supported by static visual cues but can then use sensory cues other than visual cues to roughly maintain that orientation over long time periods.
claims.source: Taken together, the data presented in this study suggest that animals need an initial orientation in the environment supported by static visual cues but can then use sensory cues other than visual cues, including wall encounters, to roughly maintain that orientation over long time periods.
claims.evidence: Inferred from observations that grid cells maintain orientation, phase, and scale in darkness after initial light exposure (Figure 6A & B).

claims.claim: For maintaining a spatial representation in a completely dark environment, vestibular signals, motor efference copies, proprioceptive feedback, and external geometrical cues may be sufficient to maintain the orientation, scale, and phase of grid cell firing fields.
claims.source: For maintaining a spatial representation in a completely dark environment, vestibular signals, motor efference copies, proprioceptive feedback, and external geometrical cues may be sufficient to maintain the orientation, scale, and phase of grid cell firing fields.
claims.evidence: Inferred from observations that grid cells maintain basic spatial properties in darkness.

claims.claim: During the light condition, static visual cues may offer additional cues to self-location since the distance and direction to these cues systematically change with the animal's movement, and optic flow may be used for refining an estimate of self-motion.
claims.source: During the light condition, static visual cues may offer additional cues to self-location since the distance and direction to these cues systematically change with the animal's movement, and optic flow may be used for refining an estimate of self-motion.
claims.evidence: Speculative explanation for improved spatial accuracy in light condition.

claims.claim: The representation of space in a cognitive map may integrate velocity signals over past time and may therefore be history-dependent and updated at a slow behavioral time scale.
claims.source: Slow changes in both the slope of the LFP theta frequency vs. running speed relationship and the spatial periodicity of grid cells after transitions between light and dark conditions suggest that the representation of space in a cognitive map may integrate velocity signals over past time and may therefore be history-dependent and updated at a slow behavioral time scale.
claims.evidence: Inferred from observed slow saturating exponential changes in grid cell stability and theta frequency slope (Figure 8).

claims.claim: The result of integrating velocity signals over time would be a representation of space which is malleable by internal memory processes.
claims.source: The result of such an integration would be a representation of space which is malleable by internal memory processes.
claims.evidence: Speculative conclusion based on observed temporal dynamics of spatial representations.

claims.claim: The observed decrease in the slope of the LFP theta frequency vs. running speed relationship is independent from the decrease in running acceleration during darkness.
claims.source: We therefore examined if the observed decrease in the slope of the LFP theta frequency vs. running speed relationship is independent from the decrease in running acceleration during darkness. If truly independent, the y-intercept of the correlation between LFP theta frequency and running acceleration is expected to decrease during the dark condition. In fact, the y-intercept of the LFP theta frequency vs. running acceleration relationship was significantly lower during darkness (t-statistic: 8.115, p=1.16×10−6, n = 15 mice, Student's paired t-test) (Figure 1F).
claims.evidence: Supported by analysis of theta frequency vs acceleration relationship showing decreased y-intercept in darkness.

claims.claim: Restricting analysis of the LFP theta frequency to running speed analysis to time points when running acceleration was near zero did not significantly change speed tuning curves of LFP theta frequency.
claims.source: Furthermore, restricting our analysis of the LFP theta frequency to running speed analysis to time points when running acceleration was near zero (0 ± 5 cm/s2) did not significantly change speed tuning curves of LFP theta frequency (Figure 1G).
claims.evidence: Supported by analysis controlling for acceleration effects shown in Figure 1G.

claims.claim: The LFP theta frequency is directly modulated by running speed.
claims.source: These data demonstrate that the LFP theta frequency is directly modulated by running speed and that the observed change in the slope of the LFP theta frequency vs. running speed relationship in darkness reflects a change in visual inputs.
claims.evidence: Supported by analysis controlling for acceleration effects (Figure 1F & G).

claims.claim: The observed change in the slope of the LFP theta frequency vs. running speed relationship in darkness reflects a change in visual inputs.
claims.source: These data demonstrate that the LFP theta frequency is directly modulated by running speed and that the observed change in the slope of the LFP theta frequency vs. running speed relationship in darkness reflects a change in visual inputs.
claims.evidence: Supported by analysis showing changes persist after controlling for acceleration and other confounds.

claims.claim: The LFP theta frequency vs. running speed relationships in light and dark became more different with elapsed time after start of light and dark epochs at a time scale of tens of seconds.
claims.source: Averaging data from 78 sessions from 14 mice, we found that the LFP theta frequency vs. running speed relationships in light and dark became more different with elapsed time after start of light and dark epochs at a time scale of tens of seconds (Figure 1H and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: Supported by temporal analysis shown in Figure 1H and supplementary figure 1B.

claims.claim: The divergence in theta frequency vs running speed relationships between light and dark appeared to be largely driven by a change in the slope as opposed to changes in the y-intercept.
claims.source: This divergence appeared to be largely driven by a change in the slope of the theta frequency vs. running speed relationship as opposed to changes in the y-intercept.
claims.evidence: Inferred from visual inspection and quantitative analysis of slope and y-intercept changes over time.

claims.claim: There was a slow increase in slope over time during the light condition (Pearson's R = 0.79, p=0.0001) and a slow decrease in slope over time during the dark condition (Pearson's R = −0.79, p=0.0001).
claims.source: This analysis revealed a slow increase in slope over time during the light condition (Pearson's R = 0.79, p=0.0001) and a slow decrease in slope over time during the dark condition (Pearson's R = −0.79, p=0.0001) (Figure 1I).
claims.evidence: Supported by correlation analysis with visual representation in Figure 1I.

claims.claim: The increase in slope during the light condition was accompanied by a small, yet significant, decrease in the y-intercept (Pearson's R = −0.77, p=0.0002).
claims.source: The increase in slope during the light condition was accompanied by a small, yet significant, decrease in the y-intercept (Pearson's R = −0.77, p=0.0002) (Figure 1J).
claims.evidence: Supported by correlation analysis with visual representation in Figure 1J.

claims.claim: The y-intercept did not change significantly over time during the dark condition (Pearson's R = −0.16, p=0.5251).
claims.source: In contrast, the y-intercept did not change significantly over time during the dark condition (Pearson's R = −0.16, p=0.5251) (Figure 1J).
claims.evidence: Supported by correlation analysis with visual representation in Figure 1J.

claims.claim: There were fast (<10 s) light-to-dark decreases and dark-to-light increases in the slope and y-intercept of the LFP theta frequency to running speed relationship.
claims.source: In addition to those slow components of change, analyzing the transition points between light and dark conditions revealed fast (<10 s) light-to-dark decreases and dark-to-light increases in the slope (Figure 1K) and y-intercept (Figure 1L) of the LFP theta frequency to running speed relationship.
claims.evidence: Supported by temporal analysis around transition points shown in Figures 1K and 1L.

claims.claim: Many neurons in the MEC show a theta rhythmic firing pattern and the frequency of theta rhythmic firing increases with running speed.
claims.source: Local field potential activity in the MEC primarily reflects the summed activity of synaptic inputs to the MEC, which is likely to be correlated with firing patterns of MEC neurons. Many neurons in the MEC show a theta rhythmic firing pattern and—similarly to the LFP theta frequency—the frequency of theta rhythmic firing increases with running speed (Hinman et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to previous work and general knowledge about MEC neuronal properties.

claims.claim: 339 out of 342 theta modulated neurons could be analyzed using the MLE model of theta rhythmic firing.
claims.source: For each neuron, an autocorrelogram model was fitted to each of those 10 s blocks of data using the MLE approach. For each of those 10 s blocks of data, the average theta rhythmic firing frequency across neurons could then be computed from the peaks of the average autocorrelogram model across neurons by taking the inverse of the first peak in the autocorrelogram model. To analyze running speed-dependent theta rhythmic firing on the population level, we first identified continuous epochs of running speed within the ranges of 0–3 cm/s (immobility), 5–10 cm/s, 10–15 cm/s, 15–20 cm/s, and 20–25 cm/s. We next used the MLE approach to model an autocorrelogram for each running speed bin of each neuron. Neurons with sufficient number of spikes resulting in at least 100 interspike intervals to compute an MLE-modeled autocorrelogram in at least one of the running speed bins were included into the analysis (n = 339 neurons).
claims.evidence: Stated as part of the methods and results for theta rhythmic firing analysis.

claims.claim: The frequency of theta rhythmic firing was significantly reduced in the dark condition (effect size: –0.381 Hz, t-statistic: –8.598, df: 4316, p=1×10–17).
claims.source: The frequency of theta rhythmic firing was significantly reduced in the dark condition (effect size: –0.381 Hz, t-statistic: –8.598, df: 4316, p=1×10–17, CI: [–0.468 –0.294]).
claims.evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of theta rhythmic firing frequency across conditions.

claims.claim: There was a fast decrease in the frequency of theta rhythmic firing when transitioning from light to dark and a fast increase when transitioning from dark to light.
claims.source: Similar to the fast initial changes observed in the slope of the LFP theta frequency vs. running speed relationship, we observed a fast decrease in the frequency of theta rhythmic firing when transitioning from light to dark and a fast increase when transitioning from dark to light (Figure 2I).
claims.evidence: Supported by temporal analysis around transition points shown in Figure 2I.

claims.claim: The observed changes in the slope of speed tuning curves are caused by changes in mean firing rate rather than changes in the running speed-dependent gain in firing rates.
claims.source: To address the question whether the observed changes in the slope of speed response curves are caused by changes in the running speed-dependent gain in firing rates or are instead artifacts of changes in the mean firing rate of neurons, we compared speed response curves between light and dark conditions after normalization within conditions as opposed to normalization across conditions. Note that normalization within conditions corrects for changes in mean firing rate between conditions. Interestingly, we found that speed response curves appeared very similar between light and dark conditions after correcting for changes in mean firing rate and conjunctive coding properties (Figure 5B &D).
claims.evidence: Inferred from comparison of speed response curves with different normalization methods (Figure 5).

claims.evidence: Inferred from observation that LFP theta frequency slope changes match grid cell stability changes over time, while single neuron theta rhythmic firing shows only fast changes.

While error accumulation could account for the observed slow decrease in spatial stability after removal of visual inputs, error accumulation cannot be the reason for the observed slow increase in spatial accuracy after reinstating visual inputs.
claims.evidence: Logical argument based on asymmetry in temporal dynamics between light-to-dark and dark-to-light transitions.

claims.claim: If signals required for grid cell firing are integrated over time, a slow increase in spatial accuracy after reinstating visual inputs is expected.
claims.source: If signals required for grid cell firing are integrated over time, however, such a slow increase is expected.

results.result: The slope of the LFP theta frequency vs. running speed relationship decreases significantly during darkness (p=2×10⁻⁶¹), while theta amplitude does not change significantly. This change is independent of running acceleration and directly reflects changes in visual inputs.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C5, C65-C68 provide converging evidence through statistical analysis (t-tests), control for acceleration confounds (C5, C66), and demonstrate that the effect is specific to visual input changes rather than motor changes. The large effect size and multiple controls strengthen this conclusion.

results.result: Changes in the LFP theta frequency vs. running speed relationship show both fast (<10s) and slow (tens of seconds) temporal components, with the slope showing saturating exponential changes over time during light and dark epochs.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C74 demonstrate temporal dynamics through correlation analysis (R=0.79, p=0.0001) and show distinct fast and slow components of change. The statistical evidence is strong with appropriate temporal binning (10s blocks) and sufficient sample size (78 sessions, 14 mice).

results.result: Theta rhythmic firing frequency decreases during darkness, with the frequency increasing with running speed in light but not dark conditions. The number of theta rhythmic neurons shows opposite speed-dependent patterns between light (decreasing with speed) and dark (saturating at ceiling).
results.evaluation: Claims C6-C8, C53-C55, C76-C79 provide comprehensive evidence using MLE modeling of autocorrelograms with appropriate statistical tests (linear mixed effects models). The analysis includes 339 neurons with sufficient spike counts (≥100 interspike intervals), and results show consistent patterns across different significance thresholds.

results.result: Phase locking of theta rhythmic neurons increases during darkness (median MRL: 0.29→0.37, p=1×10⁻³²), while each neuron's preferred phase of firing remains unchanged between conditions. Changes show fast temporal dynamics without slow components.
results.evaluation: Claims C9-C10, C81-C82 demonstrate increased synchrony with strong statistical evidence (Wilcoxon signed-rank test, p=1×10⁻³²) and stability of preferred phases (high circular-linear correlation in Figure 3C). The temporal analysis (C81) appropriately characterizes the dynamics.

results.result: Visual inputs modulate mean firing rates of MEC neurons, with 16.5% showing positive and 3.8% showing negative modulation. These changes are driven by retinal stimulation rather than spatial information content, as demonstrated by optogenetic control experiments with spatially non-informative light.
results.evaluation: Claims C11-C12, C58-C59 provide strong evidence through quantitative analysis (842 neurons, 15 mice) and critical optogenetic control experiments (Figure 4E-F) that distinguish retinal stimulation effects from spatial information processing. The ~4:1 ratio of positive to negative modulation is consistent across manipulations.

results.result: The running speed-dependent gain in firing rates of MEC speed cells remains unaltered during darkness when analyzed after normalization within conditions to correct for changes in mean firing rate. Speed scores are highly correlated between light and dark (R=0.86).
results.evaluation: Claims C14-C16, C32, C83-C84 demonstrate that apparent changes in speed tuning slopes are artifacts of mean firing rate changes. The analysis appropriately uses within-condition normalization and LN-model to control for conjunctive coding (164 neurons). This is a critical methodological contribution distinguishing gain changes from baseline shifts.

results.result: Grid cell spatial periodicity is low but not eliminated in initial darkness, increases strongly with light exposure, and remains partially elevated in subsequent darkness. Grid fields appear wider in darkness due to reduced spatiotemporal accuracy without changes in spacing (42 cm), phase, or orientation.
results.evaluation: Claims C17-C23, C85 provide comprehensive characterization using multiple metrics (grid scores, spatial information, spatiotemporal correlation) with appropriate statistics (Friedman test, Wilcoxon tests). The spike-triggered firing rate map analysis (C22-C23) elegantly demonstrates maintained grid structure with reduced precision. Sample sizes are adequate (28 cells from 6 mice for main analysis, 15 cells for spike-triggered analysis).

results.result: Head direction cells maintain their preferred direction angles in darkness (R=0.836, p=1.3×10⁻¹⁸), suggesting animals remain oriented, but tuning accuracy decreases as measured by mean resultant length (Cohen's d=0.238, p=0.0337).
results.evaluation: Claims C24-C25, C86-C87 demonstrate maintained orientation with reduced precision using appropriate circular statistics (67 cells). The high correlation of preferred angles between conditions (Figure 7B) strongly supports the inference that animals remain oriented (C86), though the small effect size for MRL decrease suggests modest impact.

results.result: Border cell spatial accuracy decreases during darkness, with border scores significantly reduced (Cohen's d=-0.4975, p=0.0325), suggesting less accurate representation of environmental boundaries.
results.evaluation: Claims C26, C88 show decreased border cell accuracy with appropriate statistics (27 cells) and moderate effect size. The inference about boundary representation accuracy (C88) is reasonable given the border score metric, though the relatively small sample size and single metric warrant some caution.

results.result: Grid cell spatial stability (spatiotemporal correlation) is strongly correlated with the slope of LFP theta frequency vs. running speed relationship (R=0.966, p=1.83×10⁻²¹) but not with the y-intercept. This correlation holds within light (R=0.825) and dark (R=0.490) conditions separately.
results.evaluation: Claims C27-C29, C33 demonstrate remarkably strong correlation between grid stability and theta frequency slope using appropriate temporal binning (10s) and sufficient data points (36 total, 18 per condition). The dissociation between slope and y-intercept effects (C29) strengthens the specificity of the finding. However, correlation does not establish causation, and the analysis is limited to 7 cells from 3 mice.

results.result: Grid cell firing appears to be a function of velocity signals integrated over past time, as evidenced by slow saturating exponential changes in spatial accuracy (tens of seconds). Error accumulation alone cannot explain the slow increase in accuracy after reinstating visual inputs.
results.evaluation: Claims C30, C63, C98-C99 present a logical argument based on temporal dynamics, but the evidence is primarily inferential. While the asymmetry between light-to-dark and dark-to-light transitions (C98) argues against simple error accumulation, alternative explanations (e.g., adaptation, learning) are not fully excluded. The integration hypothesis requires additional experimental validation.

results.result: Sensory inputs other than visual inputs (vestibular, proprioceptive, motor efference, geometrical cues) can support grid cell firing in darkness, though with reduced accuracy. Animals require initial visual orientation but can maintain orientation using non-visual cues.
results.evaluation: Claims C31, C60-C61 are supported by observations that grid cells maintain orientation, phase, and spacing in darkness after initial light exposure (C17-C18). However, the specific contributions of different sensory modalities (C61) remain speculative as they were not independently manipulated. The conclusion is reasonable but would benefit from additional experiments isolating specific sensory inputs.

results.result: Changes in theta rhythmic firing as a function of running speed are similar across different functional cell types (grid cells, head direction cells, border cells) and between putative principal neurons and interneurons, though interneurons show time-dependent decreases in theta frequency not seen in principal neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C57, C80 demonstrate ubiquitous changes across cell types using appropriate cell classification methods (spike width, firing rate) and analysis across functional categories. The cell-type specific temporal dynamics (C80) add nuance, though the functional significance is unclear.

results.result: Running speed and acceleration decrease slightly during darkness (speed: 7.7% decrease, p=0.0117; acceleration: 8.0% decrease, p=0.0070), but these small changes do not account for the observed neural dynamics.
results.evaluation: Claims C3-C4 document behavioral changes with appropriate statistics (Wilcoxon signed-rank test, n=15 mice). The small magnitude of changes and subsequent control analyses (C65-C66) demonstrate these behavioral differences do not confound the main neural findings.

results.result: The manuscript appropriately contextualizes findings within established literature on grid cells, path integration, theta oscillations, and their relationships to spatial navigation and memory.
results.evaluation: Claims C34-C52, C75, C97, C100 provide appropriate citations to relevant prior work. The citations appear accurate and support the stated claims about established knowledge in the field. This contextualizes the current findings appropriately.

results.result: The authors propose that grid cell firing may be more strongly associated with mean attractor state of rhythmic firing (LFP theta) than individual neuron rhythmicity, and suggest alternative explanations involving medial septum, head direction signals, or longer integration time scales.
results.evaluation: Claims C89-C92, C94-C96 present speculative interpretations and alternative hypotheses. While these are reasonable given the data, they lack direct experimental support. The proposals are appropriately framed as possibilities requiring future investigation (C101), but should not be considered established results.

results.result: The authors speculate that visual cues provide additional self-location information through systematic changes in distance/direction and optic flow, and that velocity integration would produce a malleable spatial representation.
results.evaluation: Claims C62, C64 are speculative interpretations without direct experimental support. While plausible, these remain hypotheses that would require additional experiments to validate.

results.result: Reductions in grid cell, head direction cell, and border cell accuracy occur concurrently during darkness.
results.evaluation: Claim C93 accurately summarizes concurrent findings from multiple cell types (Figure 7). This observation is well-supported by the individual analyses of each cell type.

results.result: The study used appropriate methods including 17 male mice (3-6 months), approved procedures, tetrode recordings from MEC, carefully controlled darkness conditions, and identified 28 grid cells, 67 head direction cells, and 27 border cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C102-C110 describe methodological details that are clearly stated and appropriate. The careful attention to ensuring complete darkness (C105-C106) is particularly important for the experimental design. Sample sizes appear adequate for the analyses performed.
